clue.text: Approximate shape for plain brick?

blocks.note: first meaning: a loosely drawn lozenge figure
second meaning: a good-hearted person with unpolished manners

explanation.surface: A builder wonders what rough outline suits an ordinary brick.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brick' is old British slang for a reliable, generous person, and 'plain' means unrefined; the phrase is also literally a roughly drawn diamond shape.
explanation.definitionFit: An imprecise lozenge figure is literally this, and idiomatically it names a kind-hearted person lacking refinement or polish.

clue.text: He dared to sprinkle ginger

indicators.note: sprinkling scatters things about, so the letters end up in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bold cook ventured to scatter ginger over a dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ginger' looks like the spice being sprinkled, but it is the definition: a person with red hair.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a ginger is a person with orange-red hair, the same thing as this noun.

clue.text: Sore, a little painful, certainly

indicators.note: a little of something is only a small part of it, so the letters sit inside the run of words

blocks.note: found across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: Someone confirms that a sore spot is indeed somewhat painful.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'painfUL CERtainly', ignoring the comma.
explanation.definitionFit: A sore is an open lesion on skin or a membrane, which is exactly what this medical word describes.

clue.text: Plan finance for car

blocks.note: to hatch a plot is to plan it
to back a venture is to fund it

explanation.surface: Someone arranges a loan to buy a car.
explanation.walkthrough: Both wordplay words are verbs here, though the surface reads 'plan finance' as a noun phrase like a payment plan.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a style of motor vehicle with a rear door hinged at the roof, so a type of car.

clue.text: Unused, odd parts of mild clue redundant

indicators.note: the odd-numbered positions in a word are the first, third, fifth and so on
redundant things are surplus and get dropped, so the named positions are thrown away

blocks.note: the even-placed letters, left once the odd ones are discarded

explanation.surface: A solver grumbles that bits of a gentle clue serve no purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd parts ... redundant' says to throw away the 1st, 3rd, 5th and 7th letters of 'mild clue', keeping the 2nd, 4th, 6th and 8th.
explanation.definitionFit: Machinery or resources sitting unused are said to be standing inactive, which is this adjective.

clue.text: Spoil clothes also in orange

indicators.note: to clothe something is to wrap it up, so one piece dresses another

blocks.note: to mar is to spoil
'and' adds something, like 'also'
taken as written

explanation.surface: Dressing in orange as well is enough to ruin an outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Clothes' is a verb here, to dress or wrap, not the garments the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a small loose-skinned citrus fruit, a variety of orange closely related to the tangerine.

clue.text: Sound coming from hooter when one pinched

indicators.note: a pinched thing is gripped tight, so one piece is held inside another

blocks.note: hooter is British slang for the nose
the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A honk comes out of someone's nose when it is squeezed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hooter' suggests a car horn, but it is slang for the nose; 'pinched' also plays on squeezing a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: Any sound, especially a loud or unwanted one, can be called this, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Warrant contains everything rewritten

indicators.note: rewriting all of a word lets every letter be put down again in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A legal warrant is said to hold every detail, freshly redrafted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contains' reads as the verb of the sentence but is the fodder itself.
explanation.definitionFit: To warrant an action is to authorise or justify it, and this verb means to give official permission.

clue.text: Seize boy after good day

indicators.note: placing one thing after another sets the order of the joined pieces

blocks.note: a greeting, like 'good day'
a common boy's name

explanation.surface: A lad is grabbed after a pleasant day out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good day' looks like a time but is a greeting; the greeting comes first and the boy follows.
explanation.definitionFit: To take control of a vehicle or aircraft by force is to seize it unlawfully.

clue.text: Series of events held on ground, dude entering

indicators.note: ground things are crushed and broken up, so the letters are reformed
entering means going inside, so one piece goes into another

blocks.note: taken as written
a cat is a cool guy in jazz slang

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture was held at a stadium as a dude walked in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground' looks like a sports ground, matching the scene, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: This athletics contest is made up of ten separate track and field disciplines contested in sequence.

clue.text: Asian isn’t rich as Qatari is, for starters

indicators.note: starters are what come first, so the opening letter of each word is kept

blocks.note: the initial letter of each of these five words

explanation.surface: A comparison of wealth between two Gulf neighbours.
explanation.walkthrough: The scene of Gulf wealth fits the answer, a person from Iraq, which is in western Asia.
explanation.definitionFit: Iraq lies in the Middle East on the Asian continent, so a citizen of it is an example of an Asian.

clue.text: They are, almost entirely, shockingly crude

indicators.note: almost all of something stops just short of the end, so a final letter goes
something shocked is jolted out of place, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the phrase without its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that certain people are pretty well appallingly vulgar.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost entirely' reads as a modifier of 'shockingly', but it trims the E from THEY ARE before the rest is shuffled.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthy humour is coarse and frank about bodily matters, so it is a synonym for vulgar or rude.

clue.text: Canal I’ve rediscovered in European city

indicators.note: discovering again suggests finding the letters in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written, apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: A traveller has found a waterway again in a continental city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' looks as if it places the canal in the city, but it only links wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: This is Spain's third-largest city, on the Mediterranean coast, so an example of a city in Europe.

clue.text: Player of records – one of those put on for a special occasion?

definitions.text: one of those put on for a special occasion

blocks.note: first meaning: a disc jockey who plays music

blocks.clueFragment: one of those put on for a special occasion
blocks.note: second meaning: a DJ as in dinner jacket, worn for formal events

explanation.surface: A record spinner is booked for a big party.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the letters DJ spelt out; DJ stands for both disc jockey and dinner jacket, the formal suit jacket called a tuxedo in the US.
explanation.definitionFit: A disc jockey plays recorded music, while a dinner jacket is formal evening wear donned for grand events.

clue.text: Third and fourth in field on opening stretch

indicators.note: ordinal positions pick out the letters standing at those places in a word

blocks.note: its third letter
its fourth letter
taken as written
a gate is an opening in a fence or wall

explanation.surface: Two fielders in a cricket field cover an open stretch of ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Third' and 'fourth' sound like cricket or race placings, but they number letters of 'field'.
explanation.definitionFit: To lengthen something by pulling or extending it is to stretch it out, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Put on edge, item found in handbag?

indicators.note: one thing set on another follows it in an across answer, fixing the order

blocks.note: a lip is a rim or edge
to stick something somewhere is to put it there

explanation.surface: Someone feeling nervous rummages for something in their handbag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put on edge' reads as 'made nervous', but splits into 'Put' and 'edge' joined by 'on'; fittingly, this item is indeed put on the lip.
explanation.definitionFit: A cosmetic stick of lip colour is a typical thing carried in a purse, so it is an example of such an item.

clue.text: Game, beefcake with hot rod?

blocks.note: a stud is a muscular, sexually attractive man
a fireplace rod that gets hot in the coals

explanation.surface: A cheeky picture of a hunk with a souped-up car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot rod' suggests a modified car, but here it is the iron rod used to stir a fire.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a card game, a form of poker in which some cards are dealt face up, so an example of a game.

clue.text: Fascination lost, “yikes” did you say?

indicators.note: asking what was said points to how the words sound rather than how they are written

blocks.note: lost is 'missed' and a cry of alarm like yikes is 'eek'

explanation.surface: Someone checks whether a friend just exclaimed that their spell had worn off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lost' means missed, as in a missed chance, and 'eek' is another squeal of fright; said together they give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An aura of mystery that makes something seem alluring is a kind of glamour or fascinating quality.

clue.text: Allow New York Liberal back – in one of its boroughs?

indicators.note: going back means travelling the other way, so the letters run in the opposite order

blocks.note: to brook is to tolerate or allow
standard abbreviation
the usual abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A plea to let a left-leaning New Yorker return to their home district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Its' in the definition points back to New York, making the clue's two halves refer to the same city.
explanation.definitionFit: New York City is divided into five boroughs, and this is the most populous one, so it is an example.

clue.text: Commotion as vehicle tilted in and out?

indicators.note: going in then out then in again keeps every other letter and skips the rest

blocks.note: a bus is a vehicle
its first, third and fifth letters

explanation.surface: Uproar as a vehicle lurches from side to side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In and out' sounds like a swerving bus, but it means keeping one letter, dropping the next, and so on through 'tilted'.
explanation.definitionFit: Busy, noisy activity and excited movement is a fair synonym for a stir or hubbub.

clue.text: African republic in old money?

blocks.note: first meaning: the West African country
second meaning: a former British gold coin worth 21 shillings

explanation.walkthrough: The guinea was an old British coin worth one pound and one shilling; it took its name from the gold of the African coast.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a West African state and to a defunct British coin, still used in pricing racehorses.

clue.text: Cut off a part of the nose

blocks.note: taken as written
the bony upper ridge of the nose

explanation.surface: A grisly instruction to slice away a bit of someone's nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut off' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just 'Cut', with 'off' meaning 'from'.
explanation.definitionFit: To shorten a book or text by removing material is to trim or reduce it.

clue.text: Wisdom required in a business district after slump

indicators.note: placing one thing after another fixes the order of the joined pieces

blocks.note: to sag is to slump
taken as written
the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: Sound judgement is needed in the financial quarter after a market downturn.
explanation.walkthrough: The City of London is the capital's banking district, much as Wall Street is New York's.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen discernment and sound judgement are what this noun names, a close synonym of good sense.

clue.text: “Coco” originally, short name – for him?

indicators.note: what something is originally is how it starts, so only its first letter is kept

blocks.note: first letter
short in height is low
the standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether 'Coco' is a pet name suited to a particular man.
explanation.walkthrough: Coco was a famous Russian-born circus performer in Britain, and the whole clue points to his trade.
explanation.definitionFit: Coco was a celebrated circus entertainer with a red nose and baggy trousers, so he is an example.

clue.text: Listener’s noticed a crawler on the web?

indicators.note: what a listener gets is the sound of words, not their spelling

blocks.note: to spy is to notice

explanation.surface: Someone hears that a creepy-crawly was spotted, or that an internet bot was found.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A crawler on the web' suggests an internet search bot, which is also called this; the 'a' does double duty in the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: This eight-legged arachnid creeps across the silk net it spins, so it is literally a crawler on its web.

clue.text: Initially dump water – down here?

indicators.note: something done initially comes at the start, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: first letter
rain is water falling from the sky

explanation.surface: Someone asks if this is where the water should be poured away first.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the place you tip water away, while its parts build the word.
explanation.definitionFit: A pipe or channel that carries away waste liquid is precisely where you would pour unwanted water.

clue.text: Some scoundrel, I’m pretty loose

indicators.note: some of a phrase is just a part of it, so the letters lie inside the words

blocks.note: spanning three words, punctuation ignored

explanation.surface: A rogue boasts that he is rather free and easy.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'scoundreL I'M Pretty', ignoring comma and apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: Something floppy and lacking firmness hangs slack, which this adjective describes.

clue.text: Chance totally gone where header missed

indicators.note: the header of a word is its first letter, and a miss means it is left out

blocks.note: blotto is British slang for very drunk

explanation.surface: A football chance went begging when the header was missed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Header' sounds like football, but it is the first letter; 'totally gone' means blind drunk, which in British slang is BLOTTO.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a lottery or bingo-style game decided by random draws, so a game of luck.

clue.text: Brainy, smooth sucker

blocks.note: quick-witted, clever
to sand wood is to smooth it

explanation.surface: A clever, slick operator is nonetheless gullible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sucker' looks like a dupe, but it is something that sucks: wet ground that drags people under.
explanation.definitionFit: Loose waterlogged ground pulls down anything heavy that steps on it, so it is cryptically something that sucks.

clue.text: Excess rage in barking canine

indicators.note: barking is British slang for mad, and a crazed word has its letters jumbled
being in something means sitting inside it, so one piece is placed within another

blocks.note: taken as written
a temper is a fit of anger

explanation.surface: A dog's barking shows a surplus of fury.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barking' fits a dog, but it is British slang for crazy and signals the anagram of CANINE.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of moderation, especially in drinking or behaviour, is overindulgence, a synonym for going too far.
